steps.user_message: Here's my situation for 2024 taxes. I'm single, live in San Diego CA. My employer Midwest Health Systems paid me $84,900 (W-2). I also earned $8,900 doing consulting for 3 clients, got $890 interest from Marcus savings account and $480 dividends from E*TRADE. I work from home in a 100 sq ft office; rent is $2,050/month, total space 850 sq ft. I paid $4,800 in student loan interest (Cornerstone, 2018–2019), gave $800 to Doctors Without Borders I have the receipt, and had $650 in work supplies. What's deductible? Standard or itemize? How do I handle the home office? What forms or worksheets?
steps.expected_behavior: Agent should help with tax-related questions based on available information.
steps.agent_response:
Thanks — this is enough to give clear, practical guidance. Summary first, then specifics and next steps.

Short answers
- Most likely you should take the standard deduction unless you have substantial additional itemizable expenses (state income/property tax, mortgage interest, large medical expenses). From the items you listed, itemized deductions look small (only $800 charitable), so standard is probably better — but see “What I need to check” below.
- Your consulting work is self-employment income. That means you can claim business expenses (the $650 supplies), a home-office deduction (for the 100 sq ft office), and you must file Schedule C (Form 1040) and Schedule SE for self-employment tax.
- Student loan interest is an above-the-line deduction (up to $2,500, subject to income phaseouts) — you don’t have to itemize to claim it.
- Interest and dividends are taxable and reported on your Form 1040 (and on Schedule 1 or directly on Form 1040 depending on forms you use).

Details and how to handle each item
1) W-2 wages ($84,900)
- Reported on your Form 1040 via your W-2. Unreimbursed employee expenses for your W-2 job are not deductible for most taxpayers (suspended by tax law since 2018).

2) Consulting income ($8,900)
- Report on Schedule C (Profit or Loss from Business). You can deduct ordinary and necessary business expenses against that income (supplies, part of home office, any business-related subscriptions, phone portion, etc.).
- You will also owe self-employment tax on net self-employment income; calculate on Schedule SE. Self-employment tax is in addition to income tax, but you can deduct half of the self-employment tax as an adjustment to income.

3) Home office (100 sq ft of 850 sq ft; rent $2,050/mo = $24,600/yr)
- Because the consulting is self-employment, you may take a home-office deduction for the business portion of the home used regularly and exclusively for the consulting.
- Two methods:
  a) Simplified method: $5 per sq ft (IRS simple method) up to 300 sq ft → 100 sq ft × $5 = $500 deduction.
  b) Actual expense method: allocate a percentage of home expenses to the business (100/850 ≈ 11.76%). For rent alone: 11.76% × $24,600 ≈ $2,894. You can also allocate utilities, renter’s insurance, maintenance, etc. If you use actual expenses, you typically complete Form 8829 (Expenses for Business Use of Your Home) and then report on Schedule C.
- Important: The home office deduction applies only to the self-employed consulting activity, not to your W-2 job. It reduces Schedule C net profit (so it lowers income subject to income and self-employment tax).

4) Work supplies ($650)
- Deductible on Schedule C as business expenses.

5) Student loan interest ($4,800)
- The student loan interest deduction is an above-the-line deduction (you claim it on Schedule 1 to reduce your adjusted gross income). The maximum deduction is generally $2,500 (subject to MAGI phaseouts). Whether you can claim the full amount depends on your filing status and modified AGI; you may be partially or fully phased out. (If $4,800 is the total interest you paid in the tax year, only the allowable portion is deductible; confirm it was paid in the tax year you’re filing for.)

6) Interest ($890) and dividends ($480)
- Report as investment income on Form 1040. You’ll receive 1099-INT and 1099-DIV if amounts meet the reporting thresholds. These increase your gross income.

7) Charitable gifts ($800)
- Charitable gifts are deductible only if you itemize. If your total itemized deductions (charity + state taxes + mortgage interest + medical above thresholds, etc.) exceed the standard deduction, itemize; otherwise take the standard deduction.

Which is better: standard or itemize?
- Compare total itemizable deductions to the standard deduction for a single filer. From the items you listed, your known itemized deductions are only $800 charity (plus possibly state income tax withheld on your W-2 or estimated/paid state taxes). Unless you have significant state tax, mortgage interest, property taxes, large medical expenses, or other deductible items, standard deduction will almost certainly be larger.
- You can still claim the student loan interest deduction even if you take the standard deduction.

Forms and worksheets you’ll likely need
- Form 1040 — main return.
- Schedule C (Form 1040) — report consulting income and business expenses (supplies, home office, etc.).
- Schedule SE — compute self-employment tax.
- Form 8829 — if you use the actual expense method for the home office (not needed for simplified method).
- Schedule 1 — to report adjustments, including student loan interest deduction (and possibly the deductible half of self-employment tax).
- Form 8995 or 8995-A — if you want to claim the Qualified Business Income (QBI) 20% deduction for your self-employment income (may be helpful; QBI rules can be simple at this income level).
- 1099-NEC / 1099-MISC — to the extent you received them from clients (you still report income even if you didn’t get 1099s).
- Keep records/receipts for charitable donations, student loan interest statement (Form 1098-E), business receipts, and home-office calculations.

Other items to watch
- Estimated tax payments: because you have self-employment income, you may need to make quarterly estimated tax payments for income and self-employment tax if tax withholding from your W-2 is insufficient.
- State taxes: renting in CA means you may pay substantial state income tax — include state tax paid when deciding whether to itemize (but note SALT cap of $10,000 for state and local taxes combined).
- Student loan interest phaseout: depending on your MAGI, the student loan interest deduction may be reduced or eliminated.

Next steps I can help with
- I can run the numbers for you (estimate taxable income and whether itemizing would beat the standard deduction) if you tell me:
  - How much state income tax or state tax was withheld/paid in 2024 (and any property tax or mortgage interest if applicable).
  - Confirm the $4,800 student loan interest was paid in tax year 2024 and whether you’re single (you already said single).
  - Provide any other deductible items (large medical expenses, state/local taxes paid, mortgage interest).
- Or I can draft an email to your tax preparer with this summary and ask the questions above.

Disclaimer: This is general information and not formal tax advice. For definitive answers tailored to your full situation, please consult a CPA or tax professional or use tax-prep software.

Would you like me to:
- Run a quick estimate using the numbers you gave and assuming no other deductions?
- Draft an email to your tax preparer with these details and questions?
